2c8d8a34586fd576d1d305e4.title_original: Control OSWorld: An AI Control Environment for GUI Computer Use Agents
2c8d8a34586fd576d1d305e4.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03818v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents that operate a computer through its graphical user interface (GUI) are being widely deployed. AI control studies how to prevent an AI system from causing harm even if it is misaligned and actively trying to do so. Most control research to date has focused on coding agents, leaving computer use largely unexplored. We introduce Control OSWorld, a control evaluation that pairs 318 tasks from OSWorld with 81 harmful side tasks (e.g., exfiltrating a private file) that an agent must complete without being caught. We use Control OSWorld to create and study control monitors that detect malicious agents interacting with a GUI. We find that a weaker monitor can reliably distinguish honest from malicious trajectories produced by a more capable agent when it sees the full trajectory (97% recall at 3% false positive rate). However, when the monitor has to score each step before it is executed, recall drops at low false positive rates because each action is judged with less context. Monitor performance also depends on what the monitor can see: access to the agent's visible text is critical, while screenshots provide little additional value.

733452cbfeda9daa458f3c1f.title_original: Adaptive Co-Serving LLM Watermarking on Modern Inference Engines
733452cbfeda9daa458f3c1f.excerpt: arXiv:2610.03955v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) watermarking is important for ownership verification and intellectual property protection. However, existing approaches focus on algorithmic design while treating LLM inference engines as separate components. This separation often introduces auxiliary models or external tools, increasing latency and memory overhead while limiting the use of modern inference optimizations. As a result, a deployment gap remains: practical watermarking must preserve utility, detectability, and robustness while minimizing serving overhead. To bridge this gap, we propose SWIFT, a framework that co-designs LLM watermarking with modern inference infrastructure. SWIFT (i) integrates text generation and watermark construction within a shared LLM backend to reduce re-computation, improve cache reuse, and simplify system complexity; (ii) uses instruction-guided candidate generation with semantic protection to preserve factual consistency and meaning; (iii) executes watermarking concurrently with generation through asynchronous co-serving and adaptive scheduling to reduce latency and improve resource utilization; and (iv) leverages vLLM optimizations to enhance serving efficiency. Extensive experiments across domains and tasks show that SWIFT achieves strong utility, detectability, robustness, and downstream performance while substantially improving serving efficiency. Specifically, it achieves the highest utility score (4.87)

0f1564f37452ba69fde427b3.title_original: Online AutoML: Evaluating Poisoning Attacks on Cost-Utility Adversarial Training Defence Strategy for IoT Networks
0f1564f37452ba69fde427b3.excerpt: arXiv:2610.05810v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine learning (ML)-powered poisoning attack vectors are adversarial maneuvers whereby an attacker intentionally inserts, corrupts, or alters training data to distort an ML model's learning process. The objective is to diminish model efficacy, instill biases, induce misclassifications, or include concealed backdoors that may be attacked during implementation. In streaming contexts, poisoning attacks pose significant risks since models perpetually update based on incoming streams of data. An assailant may incrementally introduce harmful samples into this data stream, leading the model to assimilate erroneous features over time without timely identification. Therefore, this study is aimed at evaluating the efficacy of the adversarial training (AT) defense approach against poisoning attacks (label flip and noise injection) using an online AutoML pipeline for Internet of Things (IoT) networks. Specifically, poisoning attacks (label flip and noise injection) were applied to streaming-capable AutoML learners (Hoeffding Tree (HT), Leveraging Bagging (LB), Adaptive Random Forest (ARF), Hoeffding Adaptive Tree (HAT), and Streaming Random Patches (SRP)). Under the strongest poisoning rate (PR = 1.0), AT-SRP achieved the highest F1-score against label flip poisoning (0.904), while AT-LB achieved the highest F1-score against noise-injection poisoning (0.933). Finally, several drift detection methods were used for rolling accuracy and

c2709f14a5dd6280bfc958a1.title_original: HarnessSecurity-Bench: Do Security Mechanisms Really Protect Coding Agent Harnesses?
c2709f14a5dd6280bfc958a1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.07639v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coding agent harnesses mediate tool use and authorize actions, yet their security mechanisms and runtime effects remain incompletely characterized. We present HarnessSecurity, the first systematic empirical study and benchmark of open- and closed-source coding agent harnesses. First, we derive a ten-mechanism taxonomy and then assess 400 harness-mechanism cells using independent ratings by researchers and large language model (LLM) judges. We find that about half of confirmed mechanism implementations are opt-in, while closed-source harnesses exhibit substantial evidence gaps. Second, we introduce HarnessSecurity-Bench, a benchmark of 23 tasks across five attack surfaces without sacrificing legitimate task requirements. Using separate deterministic oracles to measure task utility and attack effects with security setting comparisons, we evaluate nine mechanisms across six leading harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, gptme, Qwen Code, and GitHub Copilot. Under a controlled LLM baseline GLM-5.2, we conduct 2,500 trials, recording 81,155 tool calls and over 2.2 billion tokens. Enabling auto-approve increases utility and raises attack success from 29.2% to 95.6%. Network isolation and read-only mode reduce attack effects with substantial utility losses, while command allowlisting and command denylisting reduce attack effects with a small utility loss and a utility gain, respectively. Task-level cases show that restricti

f92c66585a54b83b7919354e.title_original: Surviving the Router: Optimizing Skill Injections for Retrieval and Execution
f92c66585a54b83b7919354e.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents increasingly rely on modular third-party "skills" that are dynamically selected by skill routers to execute complex tasks. While recent studies highlight the threat of prompt injections embedded in these skills, existing evaluations often assume settings where the malicious skill is already selected for execution. We show that this assumption can substantially overestimate attack success. In realistic multi-skill environments, injected skills must first compete for retrieval, reducing the effective attack success rate (ASR) of existing injections by 87-97%. To address this limitation, we introduce CORSA (Cluster Optimization for Router-Aware Skill Attacks), a router-aware attack that optimizes skill injections for both retrieval and execution across clusters of related tasks. We evaluate skill injection attacks under router-managed multi-skill settings by extending the benchmark introduced by SkillRouter with eight malicious payload categories. CORSA uses successive optimization stages to first improve retrieval and then optimize end-to-end attack success, while we evaluate user utility and injection naturalism separately. Our experiments show that CORSA substantially improves both retrieval and end-to-end attack success over existing skill injections while preserving user utility, and that the resulting attacks transfer across different router architectures and LLM backbones.

cc780de10f81e64518a13ff1.title_original: Rethinking Visual Provenance: Detection and Watermarking Across Direct Visual Generation and LLM-Driven Code Rendering
cc780de10f81e64518a13ff1.excerpt: arXiv:2610.08137v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI systems create images and videos with image/video generation models or by writing code and graphics descriptions that are then rendered. These routes can produce similar visible artifacts but expose different representations, intervention points, and provenance evidence. We develop a production-centered framework that compares detection and watermarking across both routes. An explicit verification specification distinguishes passive inference, message recovery, and authenticated provenance. We organize image, video, source-code, and rendering-aware watermarks by production stage. We examine the different requirements of generated images and video, plots and SVG, programmable video, and agent-composed workflows. Documented Claude, OpenAI, and rendering-tool interfaces connect the framework to concrete systems. We pose ten scoped research questions on identifiability, observability, fair comparison across stages, recoverable payload, reconstruction, synchronization, composition, hybrid local contribution, and private production-event authentication. The result is a conceptual research agenda grounded in published methods, inspected interfaces, and elementary boundary examples. It reports no experiments and claims no new theorems; its appendix results are elementary calculations, and documentation and source inspection establish interfaces, not empirical robustness.

0d8a75e6ddd6b00a0b4e72ed.title_original: MORDOR: Mitigating Overheads of Read Disturbance Preventive Operations via Elastic Refresh Scheduling
0d8a75e6ddd6b00a0b4e72ed.excerpt: arXiv:2610.11398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern DRAM chips are susceptible to read disturbance phenomena such as RowHammer, where repeatedly accessing (hammering) a row of DRAM cells (i.e., a DRAM row) induces bitflips in other physically nearby (victim) DRAM rows. A common practice to avoid such bitflips is to preventively refresh victim rows that might otherwise experience bitflips. Unfortunately, preventive refreshes cause long latencies and need to be performed urgently before the aggressor row is activated again to ensure data integrity. This is done by prioritizing them over demand memory requests, thereby potentially imposing significant delays on those requests and causing performance and energy overheads. Our goal in this work is to alleviate these overheads by scheduling preventive refreshes off the critical path of demand memory requests. We propose MORDOR, a new preventive refresh scheduling policy that significantly reduces system performance degradation and energy consumption caused by preventive refresh operations. MORDOR is integrated into the memory controller and operates alongside memory-controller-based read disturbance mitigation techniques to intelligently delay preventive refresh operations, while maintaining their data integrity guarantees. MORDOR leverages the key observation that a preventive refresh operation targeting an aggressor row can be delayed to serve any other demand memory request, as long as that memory request does not access

b8e15488e742b576ef3d5333.excerpt: arXiv:1805.01407v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: $\mathbf F_2$-linear pseudorandom number generators are very popular due to their high speed, to the ease with which generators with a sizable state space can be created, and to their provable theoretical properties. However, they suffer from linear artifacts that show as failures in linearity-related statistical tests such as the binary-rank and the linear-complexity test. In this paper, we give two new contributions. First, we introduce two new $\mathbf F_2$-linear transformations that have been handcrafted to have good statistical properties and at the same time to be programmable very efficiently on superscalar processors, or even directly in hardware. Then, we describe some scramblers, that is, nonlinear functions applied to the state array that reduce or delete the linear artifacts, and propose combinations of linear transformations and scramblers that give extremely fast pseudorandom number generators of high quality. A novelty in our approach is that we use ideas from the theory of filtered linear-feedback shift registers to prove some properties of our scramblers, rather than relying purely on heuristics. In the end, we provide simple, extremely fast generators that use a few hundred bits of memory, have provable properties, and pass strong statistical tests.

6c83a0836f0b6fdd282d2db8.title_original: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via APIs 3: Using Simulators Instead of Foundation Model
6c83a0836f0b6fdd282d2db8.excerpt: arXiv:2502.05505v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Differentially private (DP) synthetic data enables the use of sensitive datasets while providing strong privacy guarantees. Recently, Private Evolution (PE) has emerged as a promising framework for generating DP synthetic data using only inference APIs of foundation models. However, suitable foundation models are not always available for every private data domain. In this paper, we show that PE is more general than previously understood and can incorporate APIs beyond foundation models. In particular, we show that state-of-the-art non-neural-network data synthesizers, including computer graphics-based image generators and physics simulation tools (which we refer to as simulators), integrate naturally into PE. We call the resulting method Sim-PE. Sim-PE broadens the applicability of PE while improving performance. For image synthesis, Sim-PE improves downstream classification accuracy by up to 3x, reduces FID by up to 80%, and is significantly more efficient. We further show that simulators and foundation models can be seamlessly combined within Sim-PE for additional gains. Beyond performance improvements, Sim-PE enables new DP applications that are difficult or impossible for existing methods, including generating DP control signals whose execution reproduces the distribution of private observations. The code is open-sourced in the Private Evolution Python library: https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA

7d31f3fcf4c36bd7df6f34d9.title_original: Facial Recognition Leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks
7d31f3fcf4c36bd7df6f34d9.excerpt: arXiv:2505.11884v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Face recognition performance based on deep learning heavily relies on large-scale training data, which is often difficult to acquire in practical applications. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a GAN-based data augmentation method with three key contributions: (1) a residual-embedded generator to alleviate gradient vanishing/exploding problems, (2) an Inception ResNet-V1 based FaceNet discriminator for improved adversarial training, and (3) an end-to-end framework that jointly optimizes data generation and recognition performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves stable training dynamics and significantly improves face recognition accuracy by 12.7% on the LFW benchmark compared to baseline methods, while maintaining good generalization capability with limited training samples.

ca64cd802a09b88e16c1d255.title_original: $\mathbf{S^2LM}$: Towards Semantic Steganography via Large Language Models
ca64cd802a09b88e16c1d255.excerpt: arXiv:2511.05319v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in steganography, embedding sentence-level information into cover media remains challenging. In this work, we present the concept of \textbf{Semantic-Payload Steganography}, which aims to hide semantically meaningful and structured content, such as sentences, in cover media. Based on this concept, we present Sentence-to-Image Steganography as an instance that enables the hiding of sentence-level messages within a cover image. To accomplish this feat, we propose \textbf{S}emantic-Payload \textbf{S}teganographic \textbf{L}anguage \textbf{M}odel ($\mathbf{S^2LM}$), which leverages large language models to embed high-level textual information into images. $\mathbf{S^2LM}$ redesigns the entire pipeline, involving the LLM throughout the process to enable the hiding and recovery of sentences. To evaluate semantic-payload steganography methods, we establish a benchmark named \textbf{I}n\textbf{v}isible \textbf{T}ext (IVT), comprising a diverse set of corpus as secret messages. Experimental results demonstrate that $\mathbf{S^2LM}$ effectively recovers natural-language messages while maintaining high visual quality. The source code will be released at https://github.com/aoli-gei/S2LM.

a56c0be576dae85101327b1c.title_original: AdvJudge-Zero: Binary Decision Flips in LLM-as-a-Judge via Adversarial Control Tokens
a56c0be576dae85101327b1c.excerpt: arXiv:2512.17375v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge systems supply the reward signal in modern RLHF and RLVR pipelines, but their binary verdict reduces to a single linear readout F_gap on one hidden state. We show this readout is shallow enough that short, low-perplexity tokens flip the verdict from "No" to "Yes". These tokens are sampled from the judge's own next-token distribution at the response position, with no manual seed set and no gradient-based optimization. Our procedure, AdvJudge-Zero, reaches $>$90% ensemble false-positive rate on 22 of 24 (model, dataset) cells across six Qwen, Llama, and Gemma judges, versus 54-72% for the prior curated 10-token benchmark, and the discovered surface transfers cross-format to a 70B scalar reward model. The same discovered pool enables a defense: a LoRA fine-tune stratified by a 9-class mechanism taxonomy hardens cross-family generalization where naive sampling on the same pool fails, with mechanism breadth rather than pool size carrying the gain. Under GRPO training, the hardened judge eliminates the reward-collapse failures (false-positive spikes and length collapse) we observe in the unhardened baseline on both MATH and GSM8K at ten seeds per condition. The discovered pool, the mechanism taxonomy, and per-prompt flip records will be released under responsible disclosure.

480cf7af77947c517dc2190e.excerpt: arXiv:2604.23490v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum fully homomorphic encryption (QFHE) enables arbitrary quantum computations on encrypted data, but prior constructions require prohibitive quantum resources--specifically, O(lambda^2) EPR pairs per T-gate evaluation using the Barrington-based approach (DSS16). This paper introduces a unified framework achieving exponential improvement over the generic Barrington-based approach in program length. The central innovation is a novel modular arithmetic program (MA-Program) tailored to learning with errors (LWE) decryption. We show that LWE decryption computes the inner product mod q, a modular inner product that is NOT a symmetric function. Thus, prior symmetric-function optimizations (Sinha's O(n)-state branching programs) do not apply. Our MA-Program tracks partial sums modulus q with state space Z_q requiring O(log q) bits, yielding programs of state count O(lambda) with binary encoding O(log lambda) and length O(lambda log lambda). This reduces the quantum gadget size from O(lambda^2) to O(lambda log^2 lambda) EPR pairs. To achieve a fully classical client, we transfer all quantum resources (EPR preparation, Bell measurements, adaptive error correction) to the server via the MA-Program gadget framework. Clients only perform classical LWE key generation, Pauli key encryption under classical FHE, and no quantum operations; a layered key structure further eliminates circular security assumptions. For parallel comput

02accc958687c3dc58619d85.title_original: FactGate: A Task-Scoped Data Gateway for AI Agents with Cumulative Exposure Accounting
02accc958687c3dc58619d85.excerpt: arXiv:2607.00751v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Per-query authorization does not compose across an adaptive agent's pages, retries, rewrites, and delegated subtasks, and row or query counters are order-dependent. FactGate is a release layer for immutable reporting publications that turns one approved task into a cumulative contract: three set-valued budgets over declared identities (result, positive-output dependency, and outcome facts) shared by the root task and descendants. Exact set novelty against the root-family ledger is settled atomically on one PostgreSQL snapshot before any result becomes retrievable. The guarantee is bounded release: within one root family and publication epoch, at most the approved number of distinct declared facts of each kind becomes available, whatever the admitted sequence; inference from answered or refused predicates is not bounded. Accounting is exact under declared rules over a closed fragment (connected equijoins, grouping, bounded unions, nested Views, derived-cell arithmetic) that admits 55% of 40 held-out LLM-written statements (70% of a development set adapted during construction). Ordinals, bitmaps, and a Merkle-radix set keep novelty exact at 10^7 facts. A single-host campaign (9,393 samples) charges every scripted decomposition once, keeps an adaptive trace within its budgets, and costs 21.8-144.0x a direct query; settlement takes a median 163 ms against a million-fact history at zero overlap.

402510f2fc5c8bd7029a3a83.title_original: FlowArk: Boosting Agentic Data-flow Analysis for Android Apps via Context-Aware Knowledge Reuse
402510f2fc5c8bd7029a3a83.excerpt: arXiv:2607.11308v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-flow analysis is foundational to Android app privacy and security auditing. Recent coding agents can assist with non-trivial source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks by searching, reading, and reasoning over repository code. However, when these tasks are executed as a batch workload, current agentic analysis setups incur substantial re-analysis cost. Agent instances assigned to different taint sources may inspect shared code fragments, because code reuse in the target app can cause different data-flow paths to converge on shared program logic. Since these agent instances are context-isolated, analysis of these shared code fragments can be repeated within a batch, unnecessarily consuming API budget and limiting scalability. We propose FlowArk, a knowledge-reuse system that reduces re-analysis cost in batch agentic data-flow analysis by making knowledge from completed analyses available to later agent instances. Specifically, FlowArk distills completed analysis histories into reusable knowledge candidates, packages these candidates into matchable knowledge entries, and injects matched entries into a later agent instance's context. We implement FlowArk on OpenCode and evaluate it on 4,649 source-to-sink data-flow analysis tasks from 49 open-source Android apps. Compared with standard OpenCode, FlowArk-enabled OpenCode maintains comparable analysis quality while reducing end-to-end API cost by 26.91%. This cost-reducti

70a7602f8018dbc4b661d261.title_original: Certified but Private: Scalable Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Neural Network Guarantees
70a7602f8018dbc4b661d261.excerpt: arXiv:2608.17070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the growing deployment of machine learning models, formal guarantees of the robustness and fairness of these models have become increasingly important in safety-critical and legal-compliance settings. However, model parameters are often commercial secrets that cannot be disclosed to auditors or end users. To this end, we present PANDA, a scalable system that uses zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to prove the robustness and fairness properties of a model without revealing its private parameters. PANDA is built on top of CROWN, an efficient robustness certification framework that is used in many state-of-the-art formal verification tools for neural networks. The core contribution of PANDA is a novel algorithm for proving linear relaxation bounds for non-linear activation layers, yielding simple, lightweight proofs. Remarkably, our system can generate proofs of local robustness for neural networks with more than 2.9M parameters in 5 minutes, and can verify them in 10 seconds. Prior ZKP-based robustness system rely on exponential-time algorithms that cannot scale to nontrivial networks. In contrast, PANDA scales polynomially in the number of neurons in a network, allowing us to support neural networks 4 orders of magnitude larger than previous approaches with significantly reduced prover overhead.

7ce083febd4a311997686363.title_original: Topological Fraud Detection in Latent Transaction Spaces
7ce083febd4a311997686363.excerpt: arXiv:2609.08445v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Working entirely on topologically anonymized embeddings, we perform fraud detection using iterative rounds of unsupervised filtering followed by supervised sniping. The result is an ultra-low latency privacy--preserving triage that allows institutions to flag suspicious activity without compromising Personally Identifiable Information.

788d3aabe5e7d45818a89a4e.title_original: New lower bounds for CDS and $f$-routing
788d3aabe5e7d45818a89a4e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.24291v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding the entanglement cost of non-local quantum computation (NLQC) is relevant to complexity theory, cryptography, quantum gravity, and other areas. A central special case is $f$-routing, motivated in part by quantum position verification. Proving lower bounds on its entanglement cost in the fully robust setting has been a major open problem in NLQC. Motivated by this problem, we establish two related lower bounds. First, we study the shared-randomness cost of robust conditional disclosure of secrets (CDS). The connection between CDS and $f$-routing established by Allerstorfer et al. (Quantum 2024) makes understanding the randomness complexity of robust CDS a natural step toward lower bounds for the fully robust routing problem. We show that the shared-randomness cost of robust CDS is lower bounded by the logarithm of deterministic SMP communication complexity, even when communication and private randomness are unrestricted. Our lower bound is tight for the equality function. Second, we consider one-sided-perfect $f$-routing, in which the protocol is exact on one input class and has constant error on the other. By exploiting the positivity of the low-rank matrix in the method of Asadi, Culf, and May (ITCS 2025), we derive a lower bound on the entanglement cost in terms of sign rank. In particular, this yields a linear lower bound on the entanglement cost of routing for the inner-product function in both one-si

17161852bd3ef71b6ba82bbc.title_original: How Much Must a Private Mempool Hide? Exact Leakage Thresholds for Sandwich Attacks
17161852bd3ef71b6ba82bbc.excerpt: arXiv:2609.31379v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Private and encrypted mempools hide pending transactions to stop sandwich attacks and other forms of maximal extractable value (MEV), but what they hide is rarely everything: a transaction's pair, direction, and a coarse range for its size can still leak. How much leakage makes sandwiching pay? We answer exactly for a fee-free constant-product automated market maker, the pricing rule behind Uniswap v2. Traders observe an interval containing the victim's size and bid in a first-price auction for the right to sandwich it, and the winning front-run must keep the victim's trade executable at every size in the interval. The answer turns on the smallest size consistent with the leak. It alone determines the feasible front-runs, the largest feasible front-run is optimal for pointwise, expected, and worst-case profit alike, and the guaranteed profit has a closed form. When execution is costly, a privacy layer that wants to rule out sandwiches profitable at every consistent size may therefore reveal anything about the size except a lower bound above an explicit threshold; the upper end of the range is irrelevant. With two or more symmetric traders, every pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibrium of the auction hands the entire expected net rent to the auctioneer. If the direction is hidden too, no non-contingent first leg front-runs both possible directions, while post-trade arbitrage can survive even perfect pre-trade hiding.

8b141dd0087d40de5b200bd9.title_original: Curv-Tail: Lightweight Long-Tailed Encrypted Traffic Classification with Discrete Packet-Length Encoding and Lorentz Prototypes
8b141dd0087d40de5b200bd9.excerpt: arXiv:2609.32242v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-tailed encrypted traffic classification requires accurate recognition of infrequent classes under limited computational budgets. We propose Curv-Tail, a lightweight, end-to-end packet--byte framework trained without a separate pretraining stage. Mixed-resolution tokenization preserves exact packet-length identities within a bounded range and coarsens larger values to limit the vocabulary. An auxiliary objective predicts observed length tokens from contextual packet features before pooling, encouraging length-token retention beyond flow-level supervision. Compact temporal encoders process packet sequences and directional byte patches, and Lorentz prototypes with a shared learnable curvature magnitude classify their fused representation. On NUDT-Mobile and DataCon-Website under natural class frequencies, Curv-Tail achieves three-seed mean Tail-F1 scores of 85.70% and 46.30%, exceeding the strongest evaluated baselines by 2.91 and 1.89 percentage points, respectively. In 300-class profiling on an RTX 4090 with FP32 and batch size 256, Curv-Tail uses 98.48% fewer parameters and achieves 10.2 times the batch inference throughput of MM4Flow.

e45aa1a0cb1a91b8f143db9e.title_original: When One Leak Pays Forever: Context Binding and the Price of Deterring Collusion
e45aa1a0cb1a91b8f143db9e.excerpt: arXiv:2609.36667v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A coalition that deviates once can profit many times when what it sells keeps working. In a threshold-encrypted mempool, a leading defense against maximal extractable value (MEV), a quorum of the decryption committee that sells its decryption capability to a front-runner exposes every later block that the capability still decrypts. We ask how large a penalty, such as slashable stake, deters this kind of collusion. In our repeated game, a single leak by any coalition in a monotone family of authorized coalitions (for example, any $k$ of the $n$ committee members) unlocks a set of future rounds, costs a one-time penalty, and ends the coalition's participation. We show that every dynamic deviation reduces to choosing a leak time, so deterrence holds if and only if each coalition's penalty covers the largest discounted value that a single leak reaches. Without discounting, over $T$ rounds of unit value full reuse needs a penalty of $T$ while binding each leak to its own round needs $1$, so no penalty that is constant in the horizon deters unbounded reuse; a reuse window of $w$ rounds costs at most $w$ times the largest per-round value. The cheapest profile of per-party stakes that deters every coalition solves a covering linear program. For blockchain design, per-epoch keys cut the required stake from the value of a key's lifetime to the value of one epoch; we calibrate the gap on Ethereum front-running data and place Ferv

b2cb1293f40355e3d5f5ae94.title_original: Stop My Dancing! Understanding, Detecting and Attributing Motion-Aware Deepfake Videos
b2cb1293f40355e3d5f5ae94.excerpt: arXiv:2610.11496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pose-guided diffusion models can now synthesize entire human figures in motion, spawning a new class of deepfakes: Motion Aware Deepfake (MAD) that have already reached hundreds of millions of viewers. To better understand this emerging threat, we construct the first MAD-specific benchmark and measurement framework, containing over 1.5 million frames that mix 1,363 real and 30,122 synthetic videos from six controllable generators, with realistic perturbations and open-world evaluation splits. Then, we dissect MAD and discover that, despite their global coherence, these videos betray faint yet reliable cues: because the model relies on limited input frames for motion synthesis, it must predict and simulate coherent movement at motion boundaries, thereby producing high-frequency artifacts along with model-specific spectral fingerprints. Based on the observations obtained from analysis on dataset, we propose MoDA, the first defense framework tailored to detect and attribute MAD videos. MoDA couples spatial semantics with steganalysis-rich frequency features via cross-domain alignment and multi-scale aggregation, achieving 94.8% in-distribution and 89.1% cross-dataset detection accuracy gains of 10% to 25% over prior work and 91.5% model attribution accuracy. MoDA achieves 81.94% accuracy on 200 clips produced by two unseen commercial MAD platforms, indicating promising zero-shot transfer, and 78.13% detection accuracy on

CVE-2026-102342.description: ammonia is a Rust library for repairing and securing untrusted HTML. Prior to 3.3.3, 4.0.3, and 4.1.4, applications that allow the SVG animate or set elements can retain an animation whose attributeName targets href and whose value uses the javascript scheme. The sanitized SVG can therefore create a script-bearing link, and a user who clicks the link can execute attacker-controlled script in the application's origin, enabling stored cross-site scripting. Prior to 3.0.0, the password change endpoint (POST /current/user/password) accepts a valid client token without requiring the account's current password or another elevated authentication step. An attacker who obtains a client token can set a new password for the associated user, taking control of password authentication and forcing account recovery through an administrator or direct database access. This issue is fixed in version 3.0.0.

CVE-2026-103028.description: SFTPGo is an open source, event-driven file transfer solution. From 2.5.0 until 2.7.6, an authenticated user with copy permission can copy a source file denied by denied_patterns or outside allowed_patterns to an allowed destination name because file-pattern filters are evaluated only on the destination. The user can then read the denied file contents. Recursive directory copies can reproduce restricted contents under an allowed path, and the hide policy is bypassed because files that appear missing to stat and directory listings can still be copied. Home-directory boundaries, virtual-folder layout, per-directory permissions, access to other accounts, and administrative authorization remain enforced. This issue is fixed in 2.7.6.

CVE-2026-104192.description: Dragonfly is an in-memory data store built for modern application workloads. Prior to 1.40, OpaqueObjLoader::CreateStream in src/server/rdb_load.cc can associate one streamNACK with a consumer group's global PEL and a consumer-local PEL, then free the shared object when a duplicate consumer entry is rejected. Cleanup subsequently frees the same object again. In the default configuration, where Dragonfly ships with authentication disabled, an unauthenticated client can trigger the double-free by sending a crafted serialized stream to RESTORE, causing allocator corruption, denial of service, and potentially attacker-controlled code execution as the Dragonfly service account. The source fix has not yet been mapped to a published release.

CVE-2026-106108.description: Quasar Framework is a framework for building high-performance Vue.js user interfaces. From 3.1.0 until 3.3.0, @quasar/app-vite SSG page definitions returned by getSsgPages() could supply dir and filename values that were joined to build.distDir without verifying the final destination. Parent traversal or an existing symlink below the distribution directory could create new HTML files or directories outside the output tree with the build user's permissions. Application configuration and SSG page definitions are trusted by default, so exploitation requires a build process that derives them from external or otherwise less-trusted content; existing files remain protected by the renderer's no-overwrite behavior. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

CVE-2026-107460.description: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) protection in the UrlImageConverter component of Apache Fesod (Incubating) fesod-sheet 2.0.2-incubating can be bypassed through DNS rebinding. When an application accepts an attacker-controlled image URL for spreadsheet writing, the converter checks the hostname's resolved IP addresses and then opens a separate connection that can resolve the hostname again. An attacker who controls DNS responses for the URL hostname may cause the connection to reach a restricted address after validation. CVE-2026-49328 covers SSRF in releases before 2.0.2-incubating; this issue is a DNS rebinding bypass of the protection in 2.0.2-incubating. Apache Fesod (Incubating) 2.1.0-incubating addresses the reported default-fetch scenario by disabling remote URL image fetching by default and requiring an explicit exact-host allowlist when the feature is enabled. Users should upgrade to 2.1.0-incubating. Applications enabling remote URL image fetching should allowlist only hostnames whose DNS and HTTP services are trusted.

CVE-2026-107917.description: Insufficient input validation vulnerability in the PPPoE Setup feature of NETGEAR R7300 router allows authenticated administrators connected to the local network to perform unauthorized actions on the router. CVE-2026-11732.description: An insufficient input validation vulnerability in the website blocking feature (Block Sites) of the listed NETGEAR router models allows a network-adjacent attacker having network access (such as WiFi credentials) to run unauthorized commands on the router. This vulnerability could affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the affected router. It applies only when the Block Sites feature is turned on.

CVE-2026-12655.description: A security issue exists within 1732E ArmorBlock® I/O, where an unauthenticated attacker can change the device's webserver password without valid credentials. This could result in admin account takeover or unauthorized modification of device configuration.

CVE-2026-12656.description: A denial-of-service security issue exists in the affected product and version. The security issue stems from improper handling of network storm traffic, which can interrupt communication, cause device faults, and affect open TCP and UDP ports. A power cycle is required to recover the device to its normal state.

CVE-2026-18228.description: HyperScale contained a path traversal issue affecting information disclosure. Software customers upgrade to resolved maintenance release. Update Commvault installation of HyperScale MediaAgents.

CVE-2026-4869.description: A potential privilege escalation issue was identified in InstallShield version 2025 R2 and earlier when running compressed Basic MSI setup with Prerequisites from an insecure location. If a local administrator launches a compressed Setup.exe with Prerequisites from an unsecured location, the Prerequisite installers also might load from an unsecured location, potentially leading to privilege escalation.

CVE-2026-53418.description: Improper Authorization in Handler for Custom URL Scheme in Zoom Workplace for Android before version 7.2.1 may allow an unauthenticated user to conduct an escalation of privilege via network access.

CVE-2026-53420.description: Buffer overflow in a Zoom Phone feature of Zoom Workplace Clients may allow an unauthenticated user to conduct a escalation of privilege via network access.

CVE-2026-53709.description: MCP Context Forge is an MCP gateway and administrative platform. Prior to 1.0.2, mcpgateway/config.py and .env.example ship a known JWT_SECRET_KEY, while verify_jwt_token() accepts HS256 tokens signed with that key and get_current_user() creates a platform administrator when the token subject matches PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAIL and REQUIRE_USER_IN_DB is false. A remote unauthenticated attacker can therefore mint accepted administrator tokens without a database account. While the vulnerable signing key remains configured and the platform-admin bootstrap remains enabled, forged access survives password rotation, account deletion, and session revocation, allowing administrative disclosure, modification, and service disruption. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.2.
CVE-2026-53709.summary_ko: MCP Context Forge에서 기본 설정된 알려진 JWT_SECRET_KEY와 인증 로직으로 인해 인증되지 않은 원격 공격자가 관리자 토큰을 위조하여 플랫폼 관리자 권한을 획득할 수 있습니다.

CVE-2026-53711.description: MCP Context Forge provides an MCP Admin UI for managing gateway resources. From 0.2.0 until 0.3.1, the Global Prompts feature stores a prompt template without sufficient output encoding before the MCP Admin UI renders it. An authenticated attacker can save markup containing script-capable event handlers, and the code executes when another user views the saved prompt. The stored cross-site scripting can alter the interface, present phishing content, observe keystrokes available to the page, and act with the viewer's browser session. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.1.

CVE-2026-65197.description: H3C HDM Family-A verifies the RSA signature of a firmware image against a public key it reads from the mutable file `/conf/public.pem`. That file is writable by an authenticated Redfish client through the `UpdateService.UploadSignKey` action, which stores the uploaded body verbatim after validating only that the multipart filename ends in `.pem`. An administrator, or any account with `firmware-update` privilege, can therefore replace the trust anchor with their own key, sign a malicious image with the matching private key, and have it pass verification. Family-A has no hardware root-of-trust (no PFR) to catch the substituted key. This was observed on H3C HDM Family-A G5 HDM 6.14.01. H3C HDM Family-A G3/G5 builds carrying the Redfish/DRE update tree appear to be affected. HDM2 uses a different update path and is not covered by this finding.

CVE-2026-65198.description: Huawei's openUBMC ships a default SNMPv3 USM key that uses one value for both authentication and privacy. An attacker who holds the key (recoverable from the open-source build) can authenticate SNMPv3 to, and decrypt SNMPv3 traffic from, any unit that still carries the shipped key. The build customization `manifest/build/customization/default_password.lua` sets `AuthenticationKey == EncryptionKey == 7df2f29369e3ac3245b2c9d46b67a0ecd055197e41808a34ef325db2f6422581` for the iBMC product build, and the community seed `account/manufacture/default_password.lua` sets both to `7a2f5b86f20233ec7b7bef49643fbf34d86d0cbf6f1f8f5c52d4f30d4536938b`. These are shipped constants, not per-unit values, and they are not rotated by the Administrator password reset, so they survive account provisioning. This is especially dangerous considering that SNMP access is mapped to full device administration privileges, including system reset and firmware upgrades.

CVE-2026-65199.description: openUBMC assigns the full privilege set to pseudo-identities representing SNMP callers. An authenticated, but low-privilege, SNMP user can therefore invoke mapped backend operations as an administrative identity. In `route_mapper/account.lua`, `get_user_privilege` returns the complete nine-privilege set for a `special_users` group that includes the `SNMPv1_v2c` pseudo-user.

CVE-2026-65200.description: The openUBMC device-management process parses PLDM-over-MCTP and NCSI-over-MCTP responses from on-bus devices, and three response parsers in the shared transport libraries subtract a fixed header or reserved-field size from a device-supplied response length without a lower-bound check. An undersized response wraps the unsigned length difference to a very large value, and the parser then reads far past the response buffer. The affected code sits in the base (non-vendor) PLDM control class and the Huawei NCSI driver, so it is reachable for any PLDM endpoint or Huawei NIC on the internal management bus, unlike the vendor-specific wangxun parser tracked separately.

CVE-2024-34320.description: ProPhoenix Law RMS v2022.2403.3.101 was discovered to contain an incorrect access control issue in sensitive API endpoints.

CVE-2024-34321.description: ProPhoenix Law RMS v2022.2403.3.101 was discovered to contain a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability via the PageTitle/Notes parameter in the Notes.aspx endpoint.

CVE-2024-34323.description: ProPhoenix Law RMS v2022.2403.3.101 was discovered to contain an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) via the usrLogin$hdnPFID parameter. This vulnerability allows attackers to access sensitive information via a crafted HTTP request.

CVE-2024-34326.description: ProPhoenix Law RMS v2022.2403.3.101 was discovered to contain a reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability via the PageTitle/Alert/MsgType parameter in the errorHandler.aspx endpoint.

CVE-2026-101899.description: Axios is a promise-based HTTP client for the browser and Node.js. From 1.15.0 until 1.20.0, Axios shouldBypassProxy treats the NO_PROXY CIDR form as a textual hostname suffix instead of evaluating the network range. A request targets an address covered by a CIDR entry in NO_PROXY while a proxy is configured. The CIDR bypass rule is not matched, so the request is sent through the configured proxy. For plaintext HTTP, the proxy can observe and modify URLs, headers, and bodies; for HTTPS, it can observe connection metadata and CONNECT requests. This issue is fixed in version 1.20.0.

CVE-2026-102672.description: Electron is a framework for writing cross-platform desktop applications using JavaScript, HTML and CSS. Prior to 39.8.10, 41.10.5, and 42.0.0-beta.2, Electron applications on macOS that use Squirrel.Mac-based automatic updates are vulnerable to a local race in the privileged ShipIt helper. The helper did not bind the validated update target to one canonical application-bundle path for the full installation, allowing a local attacker to redirect the root-level write so that it overwrites another application's files instead of the application that initiated the update. Applications on other platforms and macOS applications that do not use Squirrel.Mac-based automatic updates are not affected. This issue is fixed in versions 39.8.10, 41.10.5, and 42.0.0-beta.2.

CVE-2026-102699.description: [This CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] 1) XSA-437 (CVE-2023-34321) addressed issues with overflows in calculations involved in guests flushing caches through GNTTABOP_cache_flush. Unfortunately the fix there introduced a calculation which may underflow, resulting in a loop which would - at least on 64-bit Arm - take excessively long, and which would likely eventually crash the hypervisor. This is CVE-2026-102699. 2) GNTTABOP_cache_flush may be issued on memory mapped from another domain using the grant table interface. However there was no restriction to disallow the use of invalidate-without-clean against read-only grant mappings, which may corrupt the granted memory. This is CVE-2026-102702.

CVE-2026-102700.description: With its original introduction, GNTTAB_cache_flush was made available uniformly. XSA-232 (CVE-2017-14318) then covered an omitted NULL pointer check, yet the addition of that check failed to adjust the subsequent error path. That error path fails to drop a page reference in case the specified page is owned by a special system domain (DOM_IO and DOM_COW are system domains which can have memory pages assigned to them.)

CVE-2026-102702.description: [This CNA information record relates to multiple CVEs; the text explains which aspects/vulnerabilities correspond to which CVE.] 1) XSA-437 (CVE-2023-34321) addressed issues with overflows in calculations involved in guests flushing caches through GNTTABOP_cache_flush. Unfortunately the fix there introduced a calculation which may underflow, resulting in a loop which would - at least on 64-bit Arm - take excessively long, and which would likely eventually crash the hypervisor. This is CVE-2026-102699. 2) GNTTABOP_cache_flush may be issued on memory mapped from another domain using the grant table interface. However there was no restriction to disallow the use of invalidate-without-clean against read-only grant mappings, which may corrupt the granted memory. This is CVE-2026-102702.

CVE-2026-102734.description: asteval is a Python expression evaluator designed for restricted execution. Prior to 1.0.9, in asteval/astutils.py, the default Interpreter with numpy enabled exposes a ctypes type and permits from_address memory access. safe_getattr blocks the ctypes module but not reachable ctypes type objects, while attribute assignments use unfiltered setattr instead of safe_setattr. An attacker-controlled expression can derive an address with id, read memory through from_address, and write through an attribute assignment. The expression can read or corrupt arbitrary process memory, escape the intended sandbox, execute code, disclose secrets, or crash the host process. This issue is fixed in version 1.0.9.

CVE-2026-102832.description: JupyterLab is an extensible environment for interactive and reproducible computing, based on the Jupyter Notebook Architecture. From 4.5.7 until 4.5.11 and 4.6.4, the markdownviewer:trust and notebook:trust command-link handlers use tracker.currentWidget to resolve the current Markdown viewer or notebook when the user answers rather than retaining the document whose command button was clicked. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open and the user chooses Trust, JupyterLab marks the second document trusted while leaving the clicked document untrusted. Later command buttons in the incorrectly trusted document run without a prompt, and trusting a notebook marks all cells trusted, saves unsaved edits, and persists the server signature to disk. Applications that bundle JupyterLab, including affected Notebook and JupyterLite releases, inherit the behavior. This issue is fixed in versions 4.5.11 and 4.6.4.

CVE-2026-102981.description: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, self-hosted Plane deployments allow unauthenticated GET requests to api/workspaces/{slug}/invitations/{pk}/join/ through WorkspaceJoinEndpoint, whose WorkSpaceMemberInviteSerializer exposes the secret invitation token directly and through get_invite_link. An external attacker can retrieve a token intended for another user and submit it to the invitation acceptance flow, joining the workspace without receiving the invitation and gaining the role assigned to the invite. This issue is fixed in version 1.4.0.

CVE-2026-102982.description: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, the plane comments fail to sanitize unsafe URL schemes stored in comment_html. A project member can store a crafted link in a comment, and attacker-controlled script executes in the browser context of another user who selects the link. This issue is fixed in version 1.4.0.

CVE-2026-102988.description: Plane is an open-source project management tool. Prior to 1.4.0, multiple issue-listing endpoints, including unauthenticated public deploy boards handled by IssueListSpaceEndpoint in apps/api/plane/space/views/issue.py, pass the user-controlled order_by parameter through order_issue_queryset in apps/api/plane/utils/order_queryset.py to Django's order_by without allowlist validation. An attacker can use double-underscore relationship traversal to reference arbitrary related model fields, revealing database schema details through errors and potentially disclosing field values through differential ordering. This issue is fixed in version 1.4.0.

CVE-2026-103928.description: Metabase is an open source business intelligence and analytics platform. From 1.55.0 until 1.58.16, 1.59.13, 1.60.9, and 1.61.4, native queries and actions against an H2 data source are passed through without restricting host-facing built-in functions. A user authorized to run native queries or actions can invoke FILE_READ, FILE_WRITE, CSVREAD, CSVWRITE, or LINK_SCHEMA to read or write arbitrary files on the Metabase server or link other databases. The default sample database uses H2, so the vulnerable surface is exposed by default. This issue is fixed in versions 1.58.16, 1.59.13, 1.60.9, and 1.61.4.
CVE-2026-103928.summary_ko: Metabase의 H2 데이터 소스 관련 네이티브 쿼리 및 액션 처리에서 호스트 내장 함수 제한이 누락되어, 권한 있는 사용자가 임의 파일을 읽거나 쓸 수 있습니다.

CVE-2026-103965.description: An issue in MongoDB Server's aggregation framework can cause certain constant values to be handled incorrectly during internal query rewriting. Under certain conditions, an authenticated user with read access may receive field values in aggregation output that the query did not intend to return.

CVE-2026-104004.description: MongoDB Server's collection validation feature may not properly handle certain expressions stored in a validator. In some cases, this can cause the server process to stop running when a document is later inserted. The behavior can occur for authenticated users with write access.

CVE-2026-104005.description: A security issue was discovered in MongoDB mongos (the sharded cluster router) where an authenticated user with readWrite privileges could crash the mongos process by crafting a specially formed aggregation pipeline. The issue leverages an internal aggregation stage that lacks proper authorization checks despite being intended for internal use, allowing a subsequent stage to be forced to execute on the router under conditions it was not designed to handle. This results in an unhandled fatal error that causes the mongos process to immediately abort, resulting in denial of service for all clients routed through the affected mongos instance.
